metadata.title: A Small Push Lifts a Car: Pascal's Principle and Hydraulics
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: How can a small push on one piston lift an entire car?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: A hydraulic jack lets a small push lift an entire car. A narrow piston on one side, a wide piston on the other, and an enclosed fluid in between. How can a small force hold up a weight so much larger than itself?
beats.new_visual_element: U-shaped vessel: narrow cylinder left, wide cylinder (five times wider) right, joined at the bottom, filled with light-blue fluid. Grey pistons cap both; a blue car with black wheels sits on the wide piston.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: hydraulic jack at rest with car on the wide piston

beats.narration_text: Push down on the narrow piston, of area A one, with a force F one. Pressure is force per unit area, so this push raises the pressure in the fluid beneath it by F one over A one.
beats.new_visual_element: Crimson downward arrow F_1 presses the narrow piston's rod; a gold line marks the piston face with label A_1; equation Δp = F_1/A_1.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: jack, car, F_1 arrow on narrow piston, A_1 marker, Δp = F_1/A_1

beats.narration_text: Pascal's principle states that a change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid and to the walls of its container. The wide piston, at the same height, feels exactly the same increase.
beats.new_visual_element: Small teal arrows appear all at once at every wall and under both pistons, each normal to the surface it pushes on; caption line 'same Δp everywhere in the fluid'.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: jack, car, F_1, A_1, teal pressure-change arrows throughout the fluid, Δp = F_1/A_1 with 'same Δp everywhere'

beats.narration_text: That same pressure now acts over the much larger area A two, so the upward force on the wide piston is F two equals A two over A one, times F one. If the wide piston has five times the area, a hundred newton push becomes a five hundred newton lift.
beats.new_visual_element: The teal arrows under the wide piston merge (ReplacementTransform) into one thick teal upward arrow F_2; the others fade. Gold A_2 marker on the wide piston face. The narrow piston sinks and the wide piston rises, carrying the car straight up. Equation F_2 = (A_2/A_1) F_1, then 100 N -> 500 N.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: jack with narrow piston lowered, car raised, F_1 and F_2 arrows, F_2 = (A_2/A_1)F_1

beats.narration_text: The force is multiplied, but the work is not. The fluid is incompressible, so the volume leaving the narrow cylinder equals the volume entering the wide one. The narrow piston travels five times farther than the wide piston rises, and F one times d one equals F two times d two.
beats.new_visual_element: Two gold displacement arrows grow simultaneously from the starting piston levels: a long one d_1 down beside the narrow cylinder, a short one d_2 up beside the wide cylinder. Equations A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2 and F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: jack displaced, F_1, F_2, d_1 long, d_2 short, F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2

beats.narration_text: A hydraulic jack creates no energy. It transmits a change in pressure through the fluid, and trades a long, gentle push for a short, powerful lift.
beats.new_visual_element: Clean held frame: narrow piston low, car high on the wide piston, F_1, F_2, displacement arrows and F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2; summary line 'MORE FORCE, NOT MORE WORK'.
